extracted.intended_audience: university press officers, researchers, science communicators, and journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for producing accurate academic press releases about health/biomedical research so they do not exaggerate findings or mislead the public. Emphasizes what to avoid (unsupportable advice, causal claims from correlational data, over‑extrapolation from animal studies) and what to include to create accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving direct advice beyond the study's claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not give direct advice to readers to change their behaviour that goes beyond what the peer‑reviewed research supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study focused on exaggeration in the form of giving direct advice to readers to change their behaviour; 40% of press releases contained exaggerated advice compared with the corresponding peer‑reviewed articles. When press releases contained exaggerated advice the news was more likely to, too (58%); when press releases did not contain exaggerated advice, rates of exaggeration in news were only 17%. Anti‑pattern: issuing press releases that state prescriptive behaviour change recommendations unsupported by the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making causal claims from correlational data
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present correlational/observational findings as causal conclusions in the press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study identified exaggerated causal claims (making causation claims from correlational data) as a common distortion; 33% of press releases contained exaggerated causal claims. When press releases contained such causal exaggeration, associated news stories contained causal exaggeration 81% of the time; when press releases did not contain causal exaggeration, news rates were 18%. Anti‑pattern: wording like 'X causes Y' when the underlying study is observational and only shows association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extrapolating animal findings to humans
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer or overstate that results from animal studies directly imply the same effects in humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors measured exaggeration in the form of inference to humans from animal findings; 36% of press releases contained such inference. When press releases did contain these extrapolations, associated news stories did so 86% of the time; when press releases did not, news rates were only 10%. Anti‑pattern: language that presents animal-model results as if human outcomes are established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve press release accuracy as a strategy to reduce misleading health news
rubrics_metrics.description: Target press release accuracy as a primary opportunity to reduce misleading or exaggerated health news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors conclude that most of the inflation detected was already present in press releases rather than originating de novo in the media, so improving the accuracy of academic press releases 'could represent a key opportunity for reducing misleading health related news.' Note: the study is observational, so causality about how changes would affect news uptake cannot be definitively proven; the study found little evidence that exaggeration in press releases increased the uptake of news overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat academic press releases as part of the scientific publication (create accountability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare press releases with the same standards of transparency and traceability as formal publications to enable peer and public accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations (from accompanying editorial) include: include named individuals from the original research paper in the press release; link the press release to the paper it promotes; present press releases as online data appendices in full view of peers; provide opportunity for feedback in the publishing journal; create an information trail and accountability among peers and the public. The editorial also suggests considering public ranking of press releases to change academic behaviour and reduce routine public mis‑information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge study design and limitations (do not overinterpret observational results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear the study design and its limitations in the press release so readers and journalists can appropriately interpret strength of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors explicitly note their work is an observational study and therefore cannot draw definitive conclusions about cause and effect. Guidance for press releases: clearly state whether the underlying research is observational, experimental, animal, or clinical, and explain limitations to avoid overstatement. Anti‑pattern: omitting design limitations or implying stronger evidence than the study provides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimise institutional self‑promotion and hype
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid framing releases primarily as institutional promotion or hype that inflates findings beyond scientific support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper points to a culture of university competition and self‑promotion interacting with journalists' time pressures as contributing factors to exaggerated claims. For press officers and institutions, criterion is to resist incentives to sensationalize results for institutional advantage. Anti‑pattern: prioritising catchy headlines or inflated claims to increase visibility at the expense of accuracy.
